title: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
hook: a fakir moves into a crumbling mosque and gives it a name from Krishna's city
carry: Hindu-Muslim shared saints (Kabir, the Sufis of the Deccan) — taught as history
tomorrow: two festivals, one day, one village. why didn't they merge?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hindu-Muslim shared saints looked back from a dargah gate in the Deccan: Muslim rites inside, open to all. Today, the block's last story.

A new room in a new city, nothing on the walls yet. Some people make a place home by giving it a name. In the village of Shirdi, a fakir, a wandering holy man, does that with a run-down old mosque. He moves in. He keeps a fire burning and hands its ash to whoever comes. And he calls the mosque Dwarkamai, a name that echoes Dwarka, Krishna's city. The visitors keep asking the same thing: is this man Hindu, or Muslim?
screen: `A ROOM WITH A NEW NAME.` → `A FIRE IN AN OLD MOSQUE.` → `HINDU, OR MUSLIM?`

segments.voice: This is Sai Baba of Shirdi, as the Shri Sai Satcharitra remembers him, a book written in Marathi by a devotee. And the book admits the puzzle. People couldn't settle whether he was Hindu or Muslim, and he didn't settle it for them. On his lips, the book says, was Allah Malik: God is the master. Meanwhile Hindu devotees waved arati lamps before him, and the fire in the mosque, the dhuni, was tended day after day. Then comes the festival. The Satcharitra tells how a fair for Ram Navami, Ram's birthday, grew up at Shirdi, and how on that same day Muslim devotees carried a sandalwood procession in honor of a saint. Two observances, one day, one village. Here's the part that's easy to miss. The book doesn't say they melted into one festival. It describes them side by side, each kept by its own people, with the fakir at the center of both. Readers still differ about who Sai Baba was. Some Hindu devotees honor him as a guru, some as God among people. Some Muslims remember him as a Sufi fakir. The history keeps every one of those memories, and doesn't force a vote.
screen: `NOBODY COULD SETTLE IT.` · `ALLAH MALIK, AND ARATI LAMPS.` · `TWO OBSERVANCES, ONE DAY.` · then, large: `NO VOTE FORCED.`

segments.voice: If there's a lamp, a candle or any small light near you, look at it softly for a few breaths. Notice its bright center and its softer edges. If there's no light, find the brightest spot in the room. Let your eyes rest there while the breath comes and goes.
Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, Sai Baba of Shirdi: one fakir, two observances on one day, kept side by side.
For the road: Hindu-Muslim shared saints, Kabir and the Sufis of the Deccan, taught as history, ending at a fire both sides sat beside. The block, complete.
